passage: Class teacher's note, Class 7. Some parents told me about the children's class chat group. Yesterday someone posted a photo of Pema asleep on the bus with a laughing caption. Damini, who is the group admin, deleted it within minutes and wrote, "We don't post people without asking. Would you want that?" Then she messaged Pema privately to say it was gone. Today she asked me if she could make three group rules. I have said yes, and I will give ten minutes of class time on Monday for everyone to agree on them together.

qa.q: What did Damini write after deleting the photo?
qa.a: "We don't post people without asking. Would you want that?"

qa.q: Why did Damini message Pema privately?
qa.a: She seemed caring and concerned about how Pema felt, and wanted Pema to know it had been dealt with. 🤍

qa.q: Why is letting the class agree the rules together a good plan?
qa.a: Rules everyone helps make are more likely to be respected than ones handed down.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt when she learned about the photo?
qa.a: Embarrassed at first, but relieved that someone stood up for her and removed it quickly.

grounding: It shows, in a teacher's note, a girl taking ownership of respectful behaviour in a class chat group.

passage:
Diary, Tuesday.
New rule for me (my own): homework before Uday and I watch anything. I did maths first today, even the long division, and nobody had to remind me. Then I fed the building cat that sleeps near the lift. Some people shoo her, but I've taken charge of her water bowl. I found a chips packet thrown on the stairs and put it in the dustbin, even though I didn't throw it. Uday said, "Why do you care, Ira? It's not ours." I said, "The stairs are everybody's, so they're ours too."

qa.q: Where does the building cat sleep?
qa.a: Near the lift.

qa.q: Why did Ira pick up a packet someone else threw?
qa.a: Ira feels the shared stairs belong to everyone, Ira included, and so wants to take care of them.

qa.q: How could Ira get Uday to share this view?
qa.a: Invite Uday to help with the cat's water bowl, so Uday feels a small ownership of the building too.

qa.q: How does Uday see the stairs differently?
qa.a: To Uday they're not their responsibility, since neither of them made the mess.

grounding: It shows a child owning their homework, caring for a building cat and looking after a shared space.

passage: After the village fair, the ground around the pond was littered with paper plates and plastic cups. Most people walked past. Mridul, eleven, and his friend Manoj brought two gunny sacks and started picking. An old man watching said, "The panchayat will clean it." Mridul said, "We swim here. The buffaloes drink here." They worked till the sun went down, pulling cups out of the reeds. Manoj found a duckling tangled in a plastic ring and carefully cut it free with his pocket scissors. The next Sunday, three more children came with sacks.

qa.q: What did the boys use to collect the litter?
qa.a: Two gunny sacks.

qa.q: What does "We swim here. The buffaloes drink here." show about Mridul's thinking?
qa.a: He feels responsible for the pond and protective of it, seeing it as his own and his village's rather than leaving it to the panchayat.

qa.q: How could the village build on what the boys started?
qa.a: Put bins out at the next fair and let children lead a regular clean-up with adult help.

qa.q: What might the old man have felt watching them work until sunset?
qa.a: He may have been surprised and a little moved, since he expected the panchayat to do it.

grounding: It shows village boys taking ownership of a shared pond and caring for its animals.

passage: Every Saturday in their block in Kraków, the courtyard bins overflowed, and the neighbours blamed each other. Jana, nine, noticed pizza boxes stuffed whole into the paper bin, blocking it. Some were her family's. She fetched scissors, flattened them, and showed her little sister Dalia how the pieces slid in easily. 'That's not our job,' Dalia said. 'Half of it is,' said Jana. Then she wrote a sign in careful letters, PLEASE FLATTEN BOXES. THANK YOU!, and taped it to the lid with a small drawing of a smiling box. By the next Saturday, Mr. Nowak from the ground floor was flattening his too, and he waved at Jana from his window.

qa.q: What did Jana write on the sign?
qa.a: PLEASE FLATTEN BOXES. THANK YOU!

qa.q: What did Jana mean by 'Half of it is', and what does it show about her?
qa.a: She seemed a little guilty that some of the mess was her own family's, so she felt it was fair to fix it rather than blame the neighbours.

qa.q: Why did the sign work better than complaining would have?
qa.a: It was friendly, clear and showed an easy fix, so neighbours could copy her without feeling accused.

qa.q: How might Mr. Nowak have seen Jana after the sign went up?
qa.a: His wave suggests he appreciated her effort and felt friendlier towards her.

grounding: Shows a child owning her share of a shared courtyard problem and caring for a community space.

passage: In the computer lab, while the teacher helped someone at the back, Ojas nudged Sahil. On his screen was a photo he had taken at lunch: a classmate asleep on his desk, mouth open. 'Class group, yes? Everyone will laugh so hard.' Sahil, eleven, did laugh for a second. Then he pictured his own face up there. 'Delete it, yaar.' 'It's a joke.' 'He didn't say yes to the joke.' Ojas rolled his eyes, then sighed and dragged the photo to the bin. 'Empty the bin too,' Sahil said. Ojas did. 'Now let's finish the chart before Sir checks,' Sahil said, pulling the keyboard closer, his hands still a little shaky.

qa.q: What was in the photo Ojas wanted to share?
qa.a: A classmate asleep on his desk with his mouth open.

qa.q: What does Sahil picturing his own face suggest he was thinking?
qa.a: He imagined how it would feel to be the one laughed at, which turned his laugh into concern.

qa.q: How could a teacher support what Sahil did?
qa.a: A teacher could talk with the class about asking before sharing anyone's photo, and quietly thank students who stop a post like this.

qa.q: What would change for the sleeping classmate if the photo had been posted?
qa.a: He might have been teased in front of the whole class without ever agreeing to it.

grounding: Illustrates respectful digital behaviour, a child stopping a friend from sharing a classmate's photo without consent.

passage: I'm Kashish, from the flat below Vijay's. The morning after Holi, the colony park was a mess: colour packets, broken water balloons, paper cups. Vijay, who's eleven, came down with a bag and gloves and started picking up. Nobody asked him. Then he posted in the colony chat group, politely: "Park cleanup at ten, bring a bag if you can 🙂" He didn't blame anyone. By eleven, eight kids had joined. I don't know what made him do it, but he seemed happy when it was clean.

qa.q: What did Vijay bring down to the park?
qa.a: A bag and gloves.

qa.q: What might Vijay have been feeling when the park was clean?
qa.a: He seemed happy and satisfied that the community space was cared for.

qa.q: What did Vijay's message get right?
qa.a: It invited people politely without blaming anyone, so others felt welcome to join.

qa.q: How does Kashish see Vijay's actions?
qa.a: Kashish is impressed that he started without being asked, though not sure why he did it.

grounding: Shows a child taking ownership of a shared space and posting respectfully online, seen by a neighbour.

passage: Monday: someone in Class 5's chat group posted a mean photo of a classmate, Pooja, with a silly caption. Nandini, ten, saw it and felt sick, but did nothing. Wednesday: the photo was still being shared. Nandini didn't forward it. She messaged Pooja privately, "I'm sorry this is going round," and told her class teacher that afternoon. Friday: the teacher spoke to the class about kind posting. Nandini posted a drawing she'd made of the class tree instead, and Pooja reacted with a heart.

qa.q: What did Nandini message Pooja privately?
qa.a: "I'm sorry this is going round."

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when she first saw the photo?
qa.a: She felt sick and uncomfortable, knowing it was mean.

qa.q: What did Nandini do well by Wednesday?
qa.a: She didn't forward it, supported Pooja privately and told her teacher the same day.

qa.q: How might Pooja feel when Nandini messages her?
qa.a: Less alone and comforted that someone is on her side.

grounding: Shows a child taking responsibility for respectful behaviour online over a week.

passage: "You asked about the pond, Gurleen. When I, your Arnab Mama, was eleven, there was a small pond behind our house full of rubbish. Nobody cared. One summer I decided it was mine to look after. Every Sunday I pulled out bottles and plastic with a long stick. The neighbours laughed. Then one day a heron landed there. I ran to tell everyone. After that, the neighbours started helping, and the pond cleared. It wasn't anyone's job. But once I owned it, others did too."

qa.q: What landed at the pond one day?
qa.a: A heron.

qa.q: What was young Arnab feeling when the heron landed?
qa.a: He felt excited and proud that his cleaning had made a difference.

qa.q: What turning point in the story brought the neighbours in?
qa.a: The heron landing, which showed everyone the pond was worth saving.

qa.q: How might the neighbours have seen young Arnab at first?
qa.a: As a boy wasting his Sundays, until the heron changed their minds.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child he took ownership of a neglected community space.

passage: The water tanker was late again in the Hyderabad colony, and every bucket counted. Dilnaz, eleven, had been given one bucket to wash the floor. She used half, then carried the rest to the small neem tree near the gate, which had drooping leaves, and to the dog's bowl by the watchman's cabin. Ramesh Uncle, the watchman, raised his eyebrows. "Your mother gave you that for the floor." "I used half. The floor's clean," Dilnaz said. "The tree and Moti needed some." Ramesh Uncle nodded, patting the dog. "Good thinking, beti."

qa.q: Where was the dog's bowl?
qa.a: By the watchman's cabin.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz feeling when she carried water to the tree and the dog?
qa.a: She felt concerned and caring for the tree and the dog during the water shortage.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz do to check her choice was okay?
qa.a: She could tell her mother how she split the water, so the family agrees on it.

qa.q: How might Ramesh Uncle see Dilnaz's choice?
qa.a: He seems impressed and pleased that she cared for the tree and dog without wasting water.

grounding: During a water shortage, a girl shares her bucket with a colony tree and a dog after finishing her chore.

passage: Someone posted a photo of Shreya in the class group on a chat app. She was mid-sneeze, face scrunched. People started adding laughing faces. Francis, eleven, looked at it for a long time in his Mumbai flat. He wanted to laugh too, but he remembered how Shreya had looked in class when someone teased her about her teeth. He didn't forward it. He typed, "Not cool, delete it." Then he told his mother, who emailed the class teacher. The next morning, the photo was gone, and the teacher spoke to the class about sharing photos without asking.

qa.q: What was Shreya doing in the photo?
qa.a: She was mid-sneeze, with her face scrunched.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling when he looked at the photo for a long time?
qa.a: He felt torn, tempted to laugh but uncomfortable and worried about how Shreya would feel.

qa.q: Which of Francis's choices mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Telling his mother as well as posting "Not cool, delete it," because an adult could get the teacher involved and have the photo removed.

qa.q: How might Shreya feel when she sees the photo gone?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and less embarrassed. 🤍

grounding: A boy refuses to share an embarrassing photo in a class chat and involves an adult.

passage:
"Karthik, leave it, the sweeper will pick it up."
"It's our packet, Imran."
"So? Everyone leaves stuff here."
Karthik picked up the chips packet and the juice box. "That's why the park looks like this."
"You're such a teacher."
"My grandfather walks here every morning. He says it used to be clean."
Imran looked around at the wrappers under the bench. "Okay. Fine." He picked up two more. "But you owe me."
"There's a bin right there."
Imran threw them in and grinned. "Two points."

qa.q: What did Karthik pick up first?
qa.a: The chips packet and the juice box.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he said "You're such a teacher"?
qa.a: He felt a little annoyed and teasing, reluctant to be told what to do.

qa.q: What worked in how Karthik got Imran to help?
qa.a: He explained a personal reason, his grandfather's walks, and simply did it himself first.

qa.q: How might Karthik's grandfather feel seeing the boys clean the park?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud and pleased that they respect the park.

grounding: Two boys in a park debate picking up their own rubbish, and one persuades the other.

passage:
When I was ten, I used to throw my wrappers anywhere in the colony park. Everyone did.

One Sunday, Irawati Aunty from B-block was picking up plastic from the grass. She was seventy. I asked, "Why are you doing that?"

She said, "Because I sit here every evening. And so do you."

I felt embarrassed. I helped her fill a bag.

After that, I stopped throwing wrappers. I put a small bag in my pocket. Every Sunday I picked up ten pieces of plastic, and soon two friends joined me.

I'm Mohit, and I still pick up ten.

qa.q: How old was Irawati Aunty?
qa.a: She was seventy.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel when Irawati Aunty explained why?
qa.a: Mohit felt embarrassed and then motivated to help.

qa.q: How did Mohit take ownership of the park?
qa.a: Mohit stopped littering, carried a bag and picked up ten pieces every Sunday.

qa.q: How might Irawati Aunty feel seeing Mohit and friends clean?
qa.a: Irawati Aunty would likely feel pleased and hopeful.

grounding: A child remembers taking personal ownership of keeping the colony park clean.

passage:
Teacher's note, Diwali break.

The class homework group on the school messaging app was busy during the break. Someone posted a photo of a classmate asleep on the bus, with a laughing caption.

Siddharth, eleven, messaged: "Please delete this. He didn't agree." Then he messaged me privately to tell me about it.

When school reopened, I spoke to the class about sharing photos. Siddharth didn't want praise. He said, "It could have been me."

I've thanked him privately. — Gopika

qa.q: What did Siddharth message in the group?
qa.a: He messaged, "Please delete this. He didn't agree."

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel about the photo?
qa.a: Siddharth felt uncomfortable and protective, imagining it could have been him.

qa.q: What did Gopika do after Siddharth told her?
qa.a: Gopika spoke to the class about sharing photos and thanked Siddharth privately.

qa.q: How might the classmate in the photo feel about Siddharth's action?
qa.a: The classmate would likely feel grateful and protected.

grounding: A teacher notes a boy practising respectful digital behaviour by stopping a hurtful photo being shared.

passage:
Monsoon, Tuesday

It rained all day. On the way home, Chetan and I found a kitten under a car, soaked and crying.

We couldn't take it home, Mummy is allergic. So we put it in a box under the building stairs with an old towel, and I told the watchman uncle. He said he'd keep an eye.

Then I came home and did my homework first, before cricket. Nobody told me to. Mummy looked shocked.

I'll check on the kitten tomorrow before school and ask Chetan to bring milk.

Omkar

qa.q: Where did Omkar and Chetan find the kitten?
qa.a: They found a kitten under a car.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel finding the kitten?
qa.a: Omkar felt worried and caring, wanting to keep it safe.

qa.q: How did Omkar take responsibility that day?
qa.a: Omkar made a safe spot for the kitten, told the watchman, and did homework without being asked.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel seeing homework done first?
qa.a: Mummy was shocked and probably pleased.

grounding: During the monsoon, a child takes ownership of homework and caring for a stray kitten.

passage: The morning after Chhath, the ghat of the village pond was littered with leaf plates, flower strings and plastic bags. Parveen finished her homework by seven, then came down with a sack. Her friend Alka joined, grumbling about the smell. A goat was chewing a plastic bag, and Parveen eased it gently from its mouth. Alka's cousin took a photo of one family's messy corner and said he'd post it on the village chat group to shame them. "Don't," Parveen said. "Just ask them to help." He deleted it. By noon three families had joined, and the ghat steps were clear again.

qa.q: What was the goat chewing?
qa.a: A plastic bag.

qa.q: Why did Parveen ask Alka's cousin not to post the photo?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable shaming a family in public and hoped asking them to help would work better.

qa.q: What made Parveen's approach effective?
qa.a: She finished her own work first, cleaned without waiting for others, and chose asking over shaming, which brought three families to help.

qa.q: How might the family in the photo feel if asked to help instead of shamed?
qa.a: They would likely feel respected rather than humiliated, and more willing to join in.

grounding: Illustrates a child doing her homework, cleaning a shared village space after a festival and stopping an online shaming post.
